# Yes — Aurora Optics is capacity constrained

Aurora Optics' laser output is constrained by a single indium phosphide (InP) wafer fab in Tucson, Arizona, and the binding bottleneck is the MOCVD epitaxy toolset, not raw wafer count.

## The constraints on the supply side

- The Tucson InP wafer fab has a stated capacity of **40,000 wafers per year** (stated January 2026).
- The same fab ran at **full utilization in Q2 fiscal 2026** (April–June 2026; reported July 30, 2026).
- Aurora has stated that **laser output cannot grow until a new MOCVD line qualifies in early 2027** (reported July 30, 2026).
- The Tucson fab is **scheduled to close by December 2026**, with laser production moving to a **contract manufacturer in Penang, Malaysia** (announced September 1, 2026). Under the announced plan, the qualifying MOCVD line in early 2027 would sit at the Penang contract manufacturer rather than in Tucson.

## The constraints on the demand side

- In Q3 2026, Aurora said **demand for 800G optical modules exceeded supply** (August 2026) — a reversal from March 2024, when Aurora had reported weak demand and elevated 800G inventories.

## Why this matters

- Customer concentration: Halcyon Networks accounted for **38% of Aurora's fiscal 2026 revenue** and is contracted to take **most of Aurora's 3.2T laser output in fiscal 2027**. The bulk of Aurora's next-generation capacity is therefore committed to a single buyer.

## Caveats and gaps in the data

- It is **not confirmed** in the retrieved data that the qualifying MOCVD line in early 2027 will physically sit at the Penang manufacturer's site — only that this is the announced plan.
- The **identity of the Penang contract manufacturer is not stated** in the retrieved data.
- **No upstream suppliers** (InP wafer, MOCVD precursor, or equipment vendors) are recorded.
- **No other named end customers** beyond Halcyon Networks appear in the data; the 800G customer set is referenced but not enumerated.
